Do not click links or open attachments unless you recognize the sender and know the content is safe. Joe, Thank you for sending this email and bringing this matter to our attention. It is very unfortunate that Tom Goodhead kept the firm leadership in the dark about the G3 facility. As Alicia and others know, we spent considerable time discussing the G3 credit facility with Tom and made every effort to close it prior to the end of June. As you may know, certain provisions within the G3 credit agreement were flagged by Tom in June as “regulatory points”. These provisions were subsequently negotiated directly between our regulatory counsel, Juliet Oliver from Kingsley Napley (who just recently left her position as Deputy Chief Executive and General Counsel at the SRA for over a decade), and PG’s regulatory counsel, Weightmans. After several weeks of negotiations, both PG and Gramercy agreed on the precise language for all of these “regulatory points”. In fact, on Tuesday, July 29, PG’s transaction counsel, McDermott, sent the attached light redline of the Credit Agreement (which does not have any changes to the “regulatory points”) to our counsel and Tom let us know that he was prepared to sign the attached July 29 draft Credit Agreement and close the facility as soon as possible. Unfortunately, Tom did not provide an operating budget for the use of proceeds under the G3 facility. This was the last open item for Gramercy to obtain our necessary approvals to close and we had been seeking the budget from PG for several months. Nick and Josh even went to London during the week of July 21 to meet with Tom personally to discuss the G3 operating budget but he did not agree to meet them in person. Instead, he dialed in by Zoom for a short time from the Netherlands and left the budget unresolved. As a result of the careful process and advice that both PG and Gramercy received from highly capable regulatory lawyers, Gramercy is comfortable that the G3 credit facility does not violate any applicable laws or disciplinary rules or place PG attorneys at risk. Notwithstanding the foregoing, Gramercy takes the concerns of the PG attorneys very seriously and would like to help build goodwill. Accordingly, Gramercy is willing to agree to the following with respect to the provisions that you cite below: Section 4.51 – Gramercy is prepared to waive our rights regarding the obligation for PG to appoint a Key Person to the board of each Stichting. Accordingly, PG is free to appoint directors in accordance with the internal governing documents of the Stichtings. Section 5.12 – Gramercy is prepared to accept PG’s proposal and has no desire to be allowed inside a Confidentiality Ring. Section 5.15 – Gramercy believes that the access to the case management system is already subject to Disciplinary Rules but please clarify if you believe differently. Section 5.43 – Gramercy is prepared to work together with PG to find alternative arrangements. Section 5.49 – Gramercy is prepared to waive our rights regarding the representation. Accordingly, PG is not in any way constrained or obligated based on this representation. Section 6.17 – Gramercy is prepared to accept PG’s proposal and make clear that regulatory obligations trump any such consents. Section 8.22 and 8.24 – As you know, these provisions address a handful of obligations in the Credit Agreement. Gramercy is prepared to agree that all PG obligations under 5.12(b), 5.49(a), 5.49(b) and 5.49(d) are subject to PG’s determination on what it considers to be its own regulatory obligations even if it conflicts with the Qualified Independent Legal Ethics Counsel. Finally, we are willing to ask our regulatory counsel, Juliet Oliver, to make herself available for any further questions that you or PG’s lawyers have with respect to the G3 credit agreement. Please do let us know if you have any questions. Regards,Marc  From: Joseph Moreno <jmoreno@pogustgoodhead.com>Sent: 07 September 2025 17:50To: Céline Gisele Beryl Barnwell <cbarnwell@pogustgoodhead.com>; Alison Webb <awebb@pogustgoodhead.com>; Anna Varga <avarga@pogustgoodhead.com>; Faranak Ghajavand <fghajavand@pogustgoodhead.com>; Felipe Hotta <fhotta@pogustgoodhead.com>; Guy Robson <grobson@pogustgoodhead.com>; Georgina Fallows <gfallows@pogustgoodhead.com>; Leila-Zoe Mezoughi <lzmezoughi@pogustgoodhead.com>; Matt Hunt <mhunt@pogustgoodhead.com>; Matthew Newbould <mnewbould@pogustgoodhead.com>; Melissa Ferrari <mferrari@pogustgoodhead.com>; Michael Burke <mburke@pogustgoodhead.com>; Priyanka Gladson <pgladson@pogustgoodhead.com>; Sarah Bingham <sbingham@pogustgoodhead.com>; Tom Ainsworth <tainsworth@pogustgoodhead.com>Cc: Alicia Alinia <aalinia@pogustgoodhead.com>; Howard Morris <hmorris@pogustgoodhead.com>Subject: Re: G3 reservations Team - Following up on the below. Per Friday’s debrief, Leading Counsel was clear that the G3 credit facility does not place any of us at risk of breaching our professional obligations. That said, you have raised legitimate points about how several provisions could impact your case strategies and day-to-day activities. While we must respect the rights of our creditors, we do not want to expend undue resources on processes that divert from our primary duty of servicing our cases and our clients. To that end, Gramercy has agreed to revisit these terms in a manner indicative of good faith and renewed confidence in the firm. The Board will continue to seek your input as this process promptly proceeds (and welcomes volunteers to collaborate on this effort). In the meanwhile, if you have continued questions or concerns do not hesitate to contact me. Thank you again for being upfront with your views on this. I look forward to working together on these matters as we implement more formalized protocols under our new business model of transparency and teamwork. Best,Joe ​​​​Joseph MorenoDirectorFrom: Joseph Moreno <jmoreno@pogustgoodhead.com>Date: Friday, September 5, 2025 at 14:00To: Céline Gisele Beryl Barnwell <cbarnwell@pogustgoodhead.com>, Alison Webb <awebb@pogustgoodhead.com>, Anna Varga <avarga@pogustgoodhead.com>, Faranak Ghajavand <fghajavand@pogustgoodhead.com>, Felipe Hotta <fhotta@pogustgoodhead.com>, Guy Robson <grobson@pogustgoodhead.com>, Georgina Fallows <gfallows@pogustgoodhead.com>, Leila-Zoe Mezoughi <lzmezoughi@pogustgoodhead.com>, Matt Hunt <mhunt@pogustgoodhead.com>, Matthew Newbould <mnewbould@pogustgoodhead.com>, Melissa Ferrari <mferrari@pogustgoodhead.com>, Michael Burke <mburke@pogustgoodhead.com>, Priyanka Gladson <pgladson@pog"}

Pogust Goodhead Can't Step Back From Lead Role On Dieselgate Trial
By Joanne
 Faulkner 

Pogust
 Goodhead must continue co-leading claims made by millions of drivers of diesel vehicles against car manufactures after a High Court judge on Friday refused to grant the firm's application to step aside from the case heading to trial on Monday. 

Justice Sara Cockeril said she is currently not prepared to grant an order that would allow Pogust Goodhead to remove its self as a joint lead solicitor law firm through an "agency agreement" with Leigh
 Day, the co-lead counsel who would take over as sole lead in the diesel emissions litigation.

The agency agreement would see Pogust Goodhead employees carry on their work under the direction of Leigh Day. But in her ruling, Justice Cockerill said the implications of approving the plan were "far from clear," particularly around the question of potential
 impacts on lawyer-client relationship.

There is also a lack of clarity around whether the Solicitors
 Regulation Authority has been asked to approve the arrangement, Justice Cockerill said.

"As matters stand at this point in time, the status quo appears to be the best course pending further clarification from Pogust Goodhead or approval of the proposed agency relationship by the SRA," the judge said. 

Pogust Goodhead asked
 the court for permission on Oct. 6 to exit its role as a joint lead firm on one of largest group claims ever bought in English legal history. The application said that recent departures from the firm, including by its co-founder and the head partner on
 the case, risk becoming a distraction.

At least five other senior lawyers, including partner Pete Gallagher — who was overseeing the firm's team on the case — have left the firm or are working their notice.

The law firm later assured Justice Cockerill that it was "fanciful" to
 suggest that the trial could be put at risk because the SRA would interfere with the agreement, according to court documents seen by Law360 on Wednesday.  The solicitors' watchdog has been engaging with Pogust Goodhead since August and has raised no issues
 about the managerial changes at the law firm and "none is anticipated," the court note reads.

In a statement sent to Law360 on Sunday, a spokesperson for Pogust Goodhead welcomed Justice Cockerill's decision "that the status quo is the best course at this time, which means that Pogust Goodhead will continue as lead solicitor, along with Leigh Day." 

"We are fully committed to successfully litigating this historic case and remain focused on the pursuit of justice for the millions of people affected by the U.K. diesel emissions scandal," the spokesperson said. 

Pogust Goodhead acts for 750,000 of 1.6 million claims in the case. Leigh Day would have taken on the lead solicitor role alone under the proposed agreement. The law firm maintains it has the resourcing capacity to continue acting as lead solicitor, and will
 continue to do so and the outcome will have no impact on the trial.

The trial, which is due to last 10 weeks, centers
 on whether five lead defendants — Mercedes-Benz,
 Renault, Ford, Nissan and the Peugeot-Citroën
 group — incorporated prohibited "defeat devices" into diesel vehicles. 

The case is Various Claimants v. Mercedes-Benz Group AG and others, case number QB-2022-002405 and others, in the King's Bench Division of the High
 Court of Justice of England and Wales.

Dear Richard, Toby, Dinah,




First of all, very nice to meet you by e-mail -- I am happy to be taking over from Michael on the Ford claim and Quantum, and look forward to working with you!




Michael is preparing an update for you regarding the PDD Trial which will be with you tomorrow. I will also send you an update on Quantum shortly. 




I write however in relation to another matter to request your instructions. This request is very similar to that in relation to Mr Gormley, whom Michael wrote to you about on 26 September. 




It has become apparent during the Sample Claimant process that one of the individuals nominated by the Defendants, Lisa Bottomley, issued two claims: one in her personal name (which is being handled by Pogust Goodhead), and one in the name of her company, Baby
 J’s Ltd (which is being managed by Leigh Day). Following review of the documentation that the client provided us, it has become clear that the appropriate claimant in this matter is Baby J’s Ltd, as it is the company that is the legal owner of the vehicle
 that is the subject of the claim being brought in this litigation.




Consequently, we have advised Ms Bottomley that she should proceed with the claim through Baby J’s Ltd and that the claim in her personal name must be discontinued.




Before we proceed with filing the notice of discontinuance, we respectfully seek your instructions to:





Discontinue Ms Bottomley’s claim in her personal capacity in the Ford Group Litigation; and
Remove Ms Bottomley from the Ford Group Register.

As with the previous discontinuance of Kenneth Gormley’s claim, we want to clarify that this action will not have any negative impact on the litigation overall. While the Defendants will be entitled to recover certain costs due to this discontinuance, it is
 likely that on account of the Anti-Avoidance Endorsement (AAE) these costs will be paid by the ATE provider, although we suspect they will reserve their right to seek these costs either form Pogust Goodhead, or from Ms Bottomley herself. This will not result
 in any financial liability for you or the other Claimants. The costs associated with this discontinuance are expected to be minimal, particularly as Ms Bottomley's claim is part of the broader litigation and the common costs will be shared across the entire
 group.




As we proceed with this process, we do not anticipate any immediate costs being incurred, and we will continue to monitor the situation closely. If you have any questions or would like to discuss this further, I am available to do so.




We kindly request your instructions to proceed with the discontinuance of Ms Bottomley's claim, as outlined above.

Dear Richard, Toby and Dinah,

 

I hope you are all well. We have finished the first week of trial on Ford and I have set out an update below. Greg Lewis, a partner at PG who is in copy,
 will write to you separately about quantum related matters.  As you will be aware from my update on 7 October 2025, I am leaving Pogust Goodhead and
Greg will also have conduct of this matter going forward.




Executive Summary




Overall, the Claimant team is content with how things have gone. You may recall I previously flagged certain potential issues with our mechanical expert
 prior to the trial. I am pleased to report that these concerns did not manifest themselves significantly to the detriment of the case. Mr Carder performed reasonably well under cross examination, provided balanced and well reasoned answers to questions put
 to him by the Defendants, and engaged in good spirits with the Judge, who appeared to very much enjoy his candour. 




Day one and two 




We opened with the Ben Jaffey KC and Tom de la Mare KC on behalf of the Claimants' cross examining Dr Marcus Davies, a calibration manager who has worked
 at Ford for the past 25+ years. 




Mr Jaffey took Mr Davies through his career at Ford before putting documents to him about how Ford calibrated their vehicles, including their deployment
 of the various Engine Control Systems ("ECS") including EGR, LNT and SCR. He also put various points to Dr Davies on what "reduction in effectiveness" actually means in real world. 




Dr Davies' evidence showed that:

1) Ford knew what had to be done to their vehicles to
 pass the regulatory test, the New European Driving Cycle ("NEDC"); and

2) Ford programmed or calibrated their vehicles to do that and little else more.




Dr Davies did not dispute this and in fact, agreed with it. When he was asked to explain why Ford later updated their vehicles to be able to perform to
 a standard that was better than just the narrow confines of the NEDC, and without changing any of the hardware in the vehicles, his answers were less than convincing. There was a dichotomy in his evidence: he suggested that Ford took years to develop engines,
 with extensive testing to establish the limits of the components to which the vehicles were calibrated but then Ford was able to update and expand the calibration of the vehicles, without changing any hardware. For example, Dr Davies was taken to documents
 showing that as far back as 2012, Ford was working to improve its EGR rates, but there was limited reason as to why they didn't implement this prior to selling the vehicles. 




Tuesday morning focus moved to two further key areas: the 6th gear issue in the Transit van, and DeSOx:

1) Dr Davies was taken to documents that shows that certain Ford Transits, when using 6th gear, as indicated by the Gear Shift Indicator, increase their
 output NOx level by over 130%. Dr Davies did not seem surprised by this. 

2) Similarly, he seemed unbothered by the DeSOx documents that were put to him. DeSOx is the terminology used to describe an issue which affects certain
 Ford vehicles with an LNT whereby the LNT catalyst becomes saturated with SOx (another noxious gas) such that it cannot effectively act to reduce NOx. Once the LNT is compromised by SOx, the vehicle spews out NOx at vast rates and so they must purge the LNT
 of SOx, by performing what are known as "DeSOx events" to cleanse the catalyst. This comes at a significant cost of fuel economy for which consumers have to pay. The Claimants' application to amend the pleadings remains outstanding, and this is due to be heard
 next year.




The Claimant team consider that nothing in Dr Davies' evidence immediately helped Ford's position. In certain respects, it assisted our case, including
 as regards updates and proof that Ford could have improved their vehicles earlier; instead Ford primarily focused on other issues such as cost and fuel economy as opposed to regulatory compliance and environmental issues. 




On day two, the Claimant software expert, Dr Markus Heitz then took the stand. As with the September hearing, the Defendants sought to criticise Dr Heitz's
 report that it duplicated work in the Mechanical expert report, and that it was beyond his remit of instruction. Dr Heitz performed well under cross examination. Ultimately, however, much of the software analysis was agreed between the experts and Dr Heitz's
 cross-examination was quite short. 




Day three and four




Day three opened with the Defendants cross examination of the Claimants' mechanical expert, Mr Dan Carder. Despite our reservations about Mr Carder, he equipped himself well over the course of the cross examination. 




The Defendants' counsel team, consisting of Neil Moody KC and Sonia Nolten KC, took turns to cross examine Mr Carder, with Ms Nolten cross examining him on SCR and other available alternative technology, while Mr Moody covered "everything else". The Defendants'
 cross examination seemed relatively light touch and they did not go into depth on much of Mr Carder's report. 




Mr Carder dealt with their questions well and enjoyed good humour with the Judge, Lady Justice Cockerill.  He came across genuine and authentic (which has been our experience of him) and the Defendants failed to probe Mr Carder on a number of tricky areas arising
 out of his report. 




Mr Moody took Mr Carder through general points of principle and his analysis of the testing results. Mr Carder rightly pointed out that he was only there to present the data and make general points about what the Defendants could have done, at one point observing
 that it was not for him to "design a new and compliant Ford vehicle for them".  There were some comments made by Mr Carder that were not ideal, including his stating that "less EGR does not necessarily mean more NOx" but this was anticipated by us as being
 an opinion that he would share and so we were unsurprised. 




Ms Nolten then took Mr Carder through the SCR technology, an area that the Claimants' case is not as strong on as other points. She made a number of observations and suggestions that Mr Carder agreed with which may be less helpful as we move into closing submissions.
 He ultimately did not agree with her suggestion that the modulation that Ford deployed was suitable  - a key point in our argument that Ford did not calibrate their vehicles appropriately. Ms Nolten also cross-examined Mr Carder about alternative technologies.
 Mr Carder performed well. 




The morning of day four had Ms Nolten finish her questioning on SCR and then move onto alternative technology, an area that Mr Carder performed well in. While he did not make any positive assertions about what alternative
 technology "Ford should" have been using in their vehicles, he was firm that "Ford
could" have been using alternative (and we say better) technology in their vehicles.
 The Defendants' line of questioning on this at times seemed to suggest that Ford should not be held to the same standard as other manufacturers who were deploying better technology, and we think the Judge took note of
 this. Mr Carder asked the same question of Ms Nolten as to "do you think that Ford couldn't do it if VW could" who declined to answer the question. 




He made a number of good points back to the Defendants in cross examination and, most importantly, the Defendants failed to interrogate him on a number of salient areas of his report which now means they go unchallenged and are accepted in evidence, which is
 important for the case. 




Our junior barrister, Ms Joanna Buckley, lead the cross examination of Prof Migliorero, the Defendants' software expert. Similar to Dr Heitz, given much of the evidence was agreed, his cross examination was relatively short, however Ms Buckley managed to get
 a number of key admissions and agreements out of Prof Migliorero, which are salient for the overall case, and important for the cross examination of Ford's mechanical expert, Professor Frederico Millo, which commences on Monday. 




It transpires that Prof Migliorero is a former student of Prof Millo and they have worked together closely over the years. Ms Buckley, in cross examination, put to Prof Migliorero that certain paragraphs in his and Prof Millo's reports were identical. Prof Migliorero
 confirmed that the wording was from his report, and it was in fact, incorrect, which we imagine will make for a mildly embarrassing position for Prof Millo come Monday when his examination commences. 




Ms Buckley elicited from Prof Migliorero that software updates and the expansion of how the ECS operates were done within the constraints of the existing hardware but the main piece was that he confirmed the reports were prepared in concert. 




Summary




We are 4 days through 6.5 days of evidence on Ford, and so far, it appears that the wind is blowing in our favour. The Judge will take her own view on the evidence and submissions, and we still have to hear evidence on PCD, Renault and Nissan, but it seems
 to be a case of "so far, largely so good". 




I will send you a further update on Wednesday to confirm how the cross-examination of Prof Millo has gone, and Greg will write to you separately about quantum trial matters.  




Kind regards,




Michael & the Ford Litigation Team

Dear Richard, Toby and Dinah,




I am writing to update you on progress towards the Quantum Trial scheduled for October 2026.






On 21 November, we filed and served Individual Particulars of Quantum ("IPQ"s) for 36 of the 40 Sample Claimants across the Pan-NOx litigation. The IPQs for the Ford Sample Claimants are attached for your reference. IPQs for the remaining
 four Sample Claimants will be filed and served on 17 December. Broadly, these IPQs:






Specify the causes of action being pursued by each Sample Claimant — for purposes of the Quantum Trial, the two causes of action being adjudicated are breach of statutory duty and (save in specific instances where time-barred) breach of contract; and


Set out particulars of the nature of each Sample Claimant's interest in the vehicle (eg, outright purchase, hire purchase, PCP, hire agreement), amounts paid, date of acquisition and disposal, etc.






On 17 December, we will be filing and serving supplements to the IPQs that either (i) specify the quantum of loss claimed in respect of these causes of action or (ii) state with particularity the steps required to particularise the loss (ie, via
 expert evidence). We have been liaising with expert advisors to determine a detailed approach to quantifying loss and are currently finalising that approach for purposes of the IPQ supplements.





On 22-23 January 2026, a first Quantum Case Management Conference ("CMC") will be held. The parties are to make applications for any matters they want determined at the CMC by 8 January 2026. The precise agenda for the CMC is not yet certain,
 but we expect to make applications on behalf of the Claimants for further disclosure from the Defendants and possibly to address other case management issues.





The remaining timetable to the Quantum Trial is very compressed, with a first tranche of disclosure to be served by the parties in March 2026, Defences to the IPQs to be served around the same time, witness statements and a second CMC in April 2026 and initial
 exchange of expert reports in May 2026.




We will keep you updated at regular intervals on progress and seek your instructions where appropriate. In the meantime, please do not hesitate to contact me with any questions or if you would like to discuss the case generally.




Kind regards,

Dear Richard, Toby and Dinah,




I hope you are all well. The Ford portion of the PDD Trial has now finished and I have set out below an update on the final 1.5 days and our overall view of how the trial went. 




Executive Summary




Coupling the cross examination of Professor Millo on Monday and Tuesday, with the update we provided last week, the Claimants are happy with how the Ford Trial has gone. Our counsel team were able to obtain significant admissions from Prof Millo that his report
 was not "intended to be misleading" as he corrected and clarified the report when in the witness box, many of which undermined the stark language he had used in his report. When considering this in tandem with how content we were following the initial week,
 it is safe to say that we believe we have done all that we could to present the Ford case in the best manner possible, and in a true and genuine light. 




As previously advised, Lady Justice Cockrill is a very difficult judge to read, however it appears that she took significant interest in the case that we put before her and we remain hopeful that her judgment will fall positively for our case. 




Day four and five (half day)




Days four and five concentrated solely on the Defendants' mechanical engineering expert, Professor Millo. He was cross examined by Mr Jaffey KC for the Claimants. 




Mr Jaffey took Prof Millo initially through his CV and relevant working experience (noting that he has worked for and with many other vehicle manufacturers over his career), before turning to his analysis of the rules surrounding the operation of the LNT. In
 what became a repetitive statement by Prof Millo, he had to apologise and explain to the Court that his report and the analysis contained within his report, was not intended to be misleading to the Court or to the parties. He repeated this statement five or
 six times during cross examination, also explaining to Mr Jaffey and the Court that his use of emotive and definitive language should be taken as stylistic (as that is how reports are written in Italian proceedings) and that there were numerous other way in
 which his analysis could have been surmised. Our interpretation of how his evidence was delivered, was that Ford had not been entirely fair to Prof Millo when assisting him with his report, and that a delta existed between them that Mr Jaffey was successful
 in exploiting and putting on show to the Court.




Prof Millo also did not help himself by taking positions that were even more extreme than Ford, or other external investigations. When discussing conformity factors (i.e. the multiplier to the amount of NOx seen on the real world as opposed to the NEDC), Prof
 Millo took the position that the conformity factors that Ford considers to be reasonable, could have been widened. Similarly when discussing the testing results obtained by investigations by the Department for Transport and the French Royale Commission, Prof
 Millo instead of accepting the results were likely caused by the SOx issue, instead chose to say it was likely something else. Similarly, he opted to criticise the driving route that the sample vehicles were put through despite having not looked at the route
 itself to analyse it. None of this endeared him to the Judge we believe. 




Whilst there were a lot of points that Prof Millo agreed with Mr Jaffey's suggestions that his report did not fully represent the picture, i.e. becuase he had not been shown relevant documentation, or because he did not consider the entire suite of tests, all
 of which is incredibly helpful and supportive of the case we are advancing, one of the main admissions we got from Prof Millo came on Tuesday morning. 




One of the main battlegrounds on Ford is the argument about what a "reduction in effectiveness" means, with Ford taking the position that just becuase one of the ECS in the vehicle is derated / modulated, this doesn't mean NOx goes up, and that you have to
 consider the ECS and all emissions (not just NOx) holistically. Our position, which is more narrow, is that ECS modulation that equates to NOx going up is a reduction in effectiveness. Ford have been careful in their position to not say that if for example

Hi Matthew,

Jamie has passed on your request to produce a draft statute bill for Hyundai–Kia.

Please find attached a template final statute bill for Hyundai-Kia, based on the format drafted by Dr Mark Friston for the Medical Product Liability cases. This structure accords with the requirements for a compliant statute bill (i.e. a complete, self-contained
 bill of costs capable of triggering time for assessment). Tom Crow will be familiar with this template having populated several versions for the Transvaginal Mesh cases.

The bill will require three schedules:



Schedule 1 – Narrative of Work Done

This schedule must provide a clear and reasonably detailed narrative of the work undertaken (see
Friston on Costs, §51.20–51.25). It must cover:


Hyundai–Kia GLO-specific work; and
Work done within the Pan-NOx coordinated proceedings that benefited Hyundai–Kia claimants.

The narrative must be sufficiently detailed to constitute a “statute bill” under s.69 Solicitors Act 1974, i.e., capable of being understood without reference to the firm’s internal ledgers.
Someone in the Hyundai–Kia legal team can compile this information.



Schedule 2 – Basic Charges

This must show a breakdown of:


Hyundai–Kia common profit costs
Hyundai–Kia individual-client profit costs
Pan-NOx common profit costs, apportioned to Hyundai–Kia using the proportionate share of 4.29% (i.e. 78,779 claims relate to Hyundai-Kia out of the total 1,836,174 across all GLOs)
(please note the percentage has been updated, so you may need to amend the ‘Copy of 2025.11.05 Hyundai Kia Demand – In Hand Compensation Model’ spreadsheet).

The common costs are based on 100% of the costs incurred (subject to assessment) and 100% approved (subject to pro-rata allocation) in the cost budgets, plus any non-budgeted costs. It does not include costs incurred beyond the approved amount.

NOTE: Please ensure that any solicitor-own-client costs are identified separately if they are to be included in the statute bill. This is not currently included in the draft. The figure will be the balance per phase, where PG has gone “over budget.”

A statute bill may include both profit costs recoverable inter partes and non-recoverable solicitor-own-client elements, provided the bill is properly itemised (Friston, §51.13–51.15). However, given the 50% damages cap in Section I of the statute
 bill, it may be that no additional solicitor-own-client costs need to be included, as the cap is exhausted (Section J). It would make for a much smoother solicitor-own-client assessment (if there was one) to base the costs on the court-approved budgeted amounts.

 

Section A – Profit Costs (figures to be used in statute bill)

The Hyundai–Kia common profit costs are derived from the attached breakdown ‘Schedule 2 Hyundai Kia & Pan NOx Basic Charges’ of the court-approved cost budgets (then we net off the paid disbursements). The position is as follows:

Hyundai–Kia Common Costs

Dear Raminder,




Please consider this a formal grievance in accordance with the firm's grievance policy (v1.0, 4 July 2024).




Acas early reconciliation process




This is a unique grievance for two reasons.  First, the grievance is with senior leadership of the firm, whom I understand will have responsibility for considering whether to uphold or dismiss it.  Second, its subject matter has been repeatedly ignored or dismissed
 by that leadership.  I therefore do not believe that it will be dealt with properly, and as set out below believe the firm has no incentive to deal with it properly.




The formal grievance process is therefore, in my view, not entirely adequate.  Accordingly, whilst I ask that you please treat this message as raising a formal grievance, please also consider it notification that I intend to contact Acas to engage the early
 reconciliation process.




Adverse health effects




The stress that I feel, and the mental health effects of PG's various reactions to the case leads' resignation, are documented in my resignation letter and various emails to the board (see, e.g., 3 October email from Michael Burke at 12:29, “we cannot stress
 enough how traumatic we and the entire team are finding this process, and that it is happening on the eve of trial”).  

 

I have not received even a bare acknowledgement of my stress, let alone any sympathy or attempt to address my concerns.  Requests for explanations and information are consistently ignored (see, e.g., 9 October email from Michael Burke at 18:14).  Attempting
 to run the PDD Trial, whilst being repeatedly distracted by the firm's behaviour, is affecting my health.  A recent example is that, on 24 October 2025, the emissions "case leads" had a meeting at which quantum resourcing was discussed.  In response to the
 suggestion that Peter Gallagher be involved, rather than a reasoned explanation be given, Anna Varga shouted that "I
[Anna] know you are all going to JLG."  The suggestion that I am motivated by some sort of conspiracy, rather than my clients' best interests, is insulting and has no basis in reality.




Having reflected, I have spoken to a mental health nurse, using my health insurance provided by the firm, for advice on how to address this stress.  The nurse advised me immediately to self-certify as off work sick with stress, and seek an appointment with
 a doctor to see if more than a week off is appropriate.

 

In any other circumstances I would do that, but at the moment I am torn as I care deeply about the trial and our clients.  The firm’s combination of silence and aggression leads me to infer that the firm, aware of my devotion to the trial, clients and colleagues,
 is anticipating that I will simply carry on regardless.  This inference only worsens my state.  Finally, whilst the firm needs me until the PCD section of the PDD Trial is complete on 28 November, from that point I believe that the firm will consider me dead
 weight.




Requested resolution




Please provide a proposal for the following:



An acknowledgement of stress that the firm's treatment of the case leads has caused.


An apology for the same.


Compensation.





The firm must have been aware of the health effects of its treatment of staff for a long time (my resignation letter explained my stress months ago), and so should be able to provide the above promptly.




I look forward to hearing from you.




Kind regards,




Matt

Chronology

- 9 October: Michael Burke sent an email to the board, on behalf of himself, me and others, explaining that we were stressed and traumatised.

- 4 November: I worked until 3am (such late hours were not unusual in trial preparation), as Anna Varga was aware from contemporaneous emails and Teams messages.

- Friday 14 November, 16:27: Sarah Bingham, who has resigned, submitted a note from her doctor resulting in her being signed off from work.
- Monday 17 November: the first day of the PCD trial.  Anna Varga sent an email to all emissions staff commenting on the amount of work done by the PCD team over the weekend.  I was exhausted, as was the entire solicitor and counsel team, and kept going.

 employment."
- As above, the firm has never before had a Sickness Absence Policy, or any policy stating that OSP is only available to employees who have not resigned.
- I was not told about the policy's introduction. No firm email or communication was sent about the policy's upload, introduction or terms.
- The firm's position is that that policy upload amounted to a unilateral change to the terms of my employment contract, without notice or consent.
- I was not told that the firm believed that the terms of my employment contract had been unilaterally changed.
- 17-27 November: I led the PCD trial for PG, attending Court every day and with conduct of the case for PG.  Ben Croft (Leigh Day partner leading PCD for LD) was unwell and only attended Court for two days, so in practice I was the most senior Lead Solicitor
 in Court with carriage of the case.  The responsibility was serious, and I took it seriously.  At the same time I worked on a handover of the PCD case to Oliver Shipway.

 this period.

- 1 December: the firm told me that I would not be paid OSP for my sick leave, and instead only SSP. The firm locked me out of PG systems, preventing me from self-certifying as fit to work, working, and thus entitling myself to pay. The firm has previously

- The consequence is that the firm is attempting to impose on me more than a fortnight of no pay. The firm has now confirmed that it does not want me to provide a handover, having previously repeatedly chased me for one.


Next steps

Kind regards,


Matt

Thank you for coming back to me and for accepting my resignation. My apologies for the delay in coming back to you, as I’m sure

Noting your comments regarding my resignation being premature, I disagree with that assessment, but we are where we are. What is

Notice Period

STRICTLY PRIVATE AND CONFIDENTIAL




Dear Richard, Toby, Dinah,




First of all, very nice to meet you by e-mail -- I am happy to be taking over from Michael on the Ford claim and Quantum, and look forward to working with you!




Michael is preparing an update for you regarding the PDD Trial which will be with you tomorrow. I will also send you an update on Quantum shortly. 




I write however in relation to another matter to request your instructions. This request is very similar to that in relation to Mr Gormley, whom Michael wrote to you about on 26 September. 




It has become apparent during the Sample Claimant process that one of the individuals nominated by the Defendants, Lisa Bottomley, issued two claims: one in her personal name (which is being handled by Pogust Goodhead), and one in the name of her company, Baby
 J’s Ltd (which is being managed by Leigh Day). Following review of the documentation that the client provided us, it has become clear that the appropriate claimant in this matter is Baby J’s Ltd, as it is the company that is the legal owner of the vehicle
 that is the subject of the claim being brought in this litigation.




Consequently, we have advised Ms Bottomley that she should proceed with the claim through Baby J’s Ltd and that the claim in her personal name must be discontinued.




Before we proceed with filing the notice of discontinuance, we respectfully seek your instructions to:





Discontinue Ms Bottomley’s claim in her personal capacity in the Ford Group Litigation; and
Remove Ms Bottomley from the Ford Group Register.

As with the previous discontinuance of Kenneth Gormley’s claim, we want to clarify that this action will not have any negative impact on the litigation overall. While the Defendants will be entitled to recover certain costs due to this discontinuance, it is
 likely that on account of the Anti-Avoidance Endorsement (AAE) these costs will be paid by the ATE provider, although we suspect they will reserve their right to seek these costs either form Pogust Goodhead, or from Ms Bottomley herself. This will not result
 in any financial liability for you or the other Claimants. The costs associated with this discontinuance are expected to be minimal, particularly as Ms Bottomley's claim is part of the broader litigation and the common costs will be shared across the entire
 group.




As we proceed with this process, we do not anticipate any immediate costs being incurred, and we will continue to monitor the situation closely. If you have any questions or would like to discuss this further, I am available to do so.




We kindly request your instructions to proceed with the discontinuance of Ms Bottomley's claim, as outlined above.




Kind regards,












​​​​Greg LewisPartner

STRICTLY PRIVATE AND CONFIDENTIAL




Dear Richard, Toby and Dinah,

 

I hope you are all well. We have finished the first week of trial on Ford and I have set out an update below. Greg Lewis, a partner at PG who is in copy,
 will write to you separately about quantum related matters.  As you will be aware from my update on 7 October 2025, I am leaving Pogust Goodhead and
Greg will also have conduct of this matter going forward.




Executive Summary




Overall, the Claimant team is content with how things have gone. You may recall I previously flagged certain potential issues with our mechanical expert
 prior to the trial. I am pleased to report that these concerns did not manifest themselves significantly to the detriment of the case. Mr Carder performed reasonably well under cross examination, provided balanced and well reasoned answers to questions put
 to him by the Defendants, and engaged in good spirits with the Judge, who appeared to very much enjoy his candour. 




Day one and two 




We opened with the Ben Jaffey KC and Tom de la Mare KC on behalf of the Claimants' cross examining Dr Marcus Davies, a calibration manager who has worked
 at Ford for the past 25+ years. 




Mr Jaffey took Mr Davies through his career at Ford before putting documents to him about how Ford calibrated their vehicles, including their deployment
 of the various Engine Control Systems ("ECS") including EGR, LNT and SCR. He also put various points to Dr Davies on what "reduction in effectiveness" actually means in real world. 




Dr Davies' evidence showed that:

1) Ford knew what had to be done to their vehicles to
 pass the regulatory test, the New European Driving Cycle ("NEDC"); and

2) Ford programmed or calibrated their vehicles to do that and little else more.




Dr Davies did not dispute this and in fact, agreed with it. When he was asked to explain why Ford later updated their vehicles to be able to perform to
 a standard that was better than just the narrow confines of the NEDC, and without changing any of the hardware in the vehicles, his answers were less than convincing. There was a dichotomy in his evidence: he suggested that Ford took years to develop engines,
 with extensive testing to establish the limits of the components to which the vehicles were calibrated but then Ford was able to update and expand the calibration of the vehicles, without changing any hardware. For example, Dr Davies was taken to documents
 showing that as far back as 2012, Ford was working to improve its EGR rates, but there was limited reason as to why they didn't implement this prior to selling the vehicles. 




Tuesday morning focus moved to two further key areas: the 6th gear issue in the Transit van, and DeSOx:

1) Dr Davies was taken to documents that shows that certain Ford Transits, when using 6th gear, as indicated by the Gear Shift Indicator, increase their
 output NOx level by over 130%. Dr Davies did not seem surprised by this. 

2) Similarly, he seemed unbothered by the DeSOx documents that were put to him. DeSOx is the terminology used to describe an issue which affects certain
 Ford vehicles with an LNT whereby the LNT catalyst becomes saturated with SOx (another noxious gas) such that it cannot effectively act to reduce NOx. Once the LNT is compromised by SOx, the vehicle spews out NOx at vast rates and so they must purge the LNT
 of SOx, by performing what are known as "DeSOx events" to cleanse the catalyst. This comes at a significant cost of fuel economy for which consumers have to pay. The Claimants' application to amend the pleadings remains outstanding, and this is due to be heard
 next year.




The Claimant team consider that nothing in Dr Davies' evidence immediately helped Ford's position. In certain respects, it assisted our case, including
 as regards updates and proof that Ford could have improved their vehicles earlier; instead Ford primarily focused on other issues such as cost and fuel economy as opposed to regulatory compliance and environmental issues. 




On day two, the Claimant software expert, Dr Markus Heitz then took the stand. As with the September hearing, the Defendants sought to criticise Dr Heitz's
 report that it duplicated work in the Mechanical expert report, and that it was beyond his remit of instruction. Dr Heitz performed well under cross examination. Ultimately, however, much of the software analysis was agreed between the experts and Dr Heitz's
 cross-examination was quite short. 




Day three and four




Day three opened with the Defendants cross examination of the Claimants' mechanical expert, Mr Dan Carder. Despite our reservations about Mr Carder, he equipped himself well over the course of the cross examination. 




The Defendants' counsel team, consisting of Neil Moody KC and Sonia Nolten KC, took turns to cross examine Mr Carder, with Ms Nolten cross examining him on SCR and other available alternative technology, while Mr Moody covered "everything else". The Defendants'
 cross examination seemed relatively light touch and they did not go into depth on much of Mr Carder's report. 




Mr Carder dealt with their questions well and enjoyed good humour with the Judge, Lady Justice Cockerill.  He came across genuine and authentic (which has been our experience of him) and the Defendants failed to probe Mr Carder on a number of tricky areas arising
 out of his report. 




Mr Moody took Mr Carder through general points of principle and his analysis of the testing results. Mr Carder rightly pointed out that he was only there to present the data and make general points about what the Defendants could have done, at one point observing
 that it was not for him to "design a new and compliant Ford vehicle for them".  There were some comments made by Mr Carder that were not ideal, including his stating that "less EGR does not necessarily mean more NOx" but this was anticipated by us as being
 an opinion that he would share and so we were unsurprised. 




Ms Nolten then took Mr Carder through the SCR technology, an area that the Claimants' case is not as strong on as other points. She made a number of observations and suggestions that Mr Carder agreed with which may be less helpful as we move into closing submissions.
 He ultimately did not agree with her suggestion that the modulation that Ford deployed was suitable  - a key point in our argument that Ford did not calibrate their vehicles appropriately. Ms Nolten also cross-examined Mr Carder about alternative technologies.
 Mr Carder performed well. 




The morning of day four had Ms Nolten finish her questioning on SCR and then move onto alternative technology, an area that Mr Carder performed well in. While he did not make any positive assertions about what alternative
 technology "Ford should" have been using in their vehicles, he was firm that "Ford
could" have been using alternative (and we say better) technology in their vehicles.
 The Defendants' line of questioning on this at times seemed to suggest that Ford should not be held to the same standard as other manufacturers who were deploying better technology, and we think the Judge took note of
 this. Mr Carder asked the same question of Ms Nolten as to "do you think that Ford couldn't do it if VW could" who declined to answer the question. 




He made a number of good points back to the Defendants in cross examination and, most importantly, the Defendants failed to interrogate him on a number of salient areas of his report which now means they go unchallenged and are accepted in evidence, which is
 important for the case. 




Our junior barrister, Ms Joanna Buckley, lead the cross examination of Prof Migliorero, the Defendants' software expert. Similar to Dr Heitz, given much of the evidence was agreed, his cross examination was relatively short, however Ms Buckley managed to get
 a number of key admissions and agreements out of Prof Migliorero, which are salient for the overall case, and important for the cross examination of Ford's mechanical expert, Professor Frederico Millo, which commences on Monday. 




It transpires that Prof Migliorero is a former student of Prof Millo and they have worked together closely over the years. Ms Buckley, in cross examination, put to Prof Migliorero that certain paragraphs in his and Prof Millo's reports were identical. Prof Migliorero
 confirmed that the wording was from his report, and it was in fact, incorrect, which we imagine will make for a mildly embarrassing position for Prof Millo come Monday when his examination commences. 




Ms Buckley elicited from Prof Migliorero that software updates and the expansion of how the ECS operates were done within the constraints of the existing hardware but the main piece was that he confirmed the reports were prepared in concert. 




Summary




We are 4 days through 6.5 days of evidence on Ford, and so far, it appears that the wind is blowing in our favour. The Judge will take her own view on the evidence and submissions, and we still have to hear evidence on PCD, Renault and Nissan, but it seems
 to be a case of "so far, largely so good". 




I will send you a further update on Wednesday to confirm how the cross-examination of Prof Millo has gone, and Greg will write to you separately about quantum trial matters.  




Kind regards,




Michael & the Ford Litigation Team

Morning Sarah,
 
Ahead of our call to discuss at 11:30am, I just thought I’d flag some initial thoughts on the below, which we can then discuss later.
 
Wording of draft Order
Happy to discuss later this morning, but from my perspective, I’m not too concerned by Ds’ drafting of para 3.
For Experts, it seems to me inevitable that the court will want to budget them once the question of disciplines is resolved (and will want to whatever the wording of the order).
For ADR, wouldn’t it be in the Claimants’ favour
not to budget (given the scale of our estimates, and the likely approach which the court would take to them), if the court had any inclination not to do so? If so, don’t we want to give room for the court to decide that ADR is actually too difficult/uncertain
 to budget at the moment, rather than say they are forced to do so?
If that’s right, I would be inclined to go with Ds’ version of paragraph 3. But happy to discuss on our call.
 
CMH2 Consequentials
This has reminded me – have we had a decision on the CMH costs order yet?
 
Timing of CMH3 (Or CMH2.2, however we want to think of it!)
I agree that if there is to be further budgeting post-January we will need to crack on with it, there’s no point trying to drag our heels.
However, query whether a Feb CMH is a bit ambitious. Presumably we need time, post Jan CMC to:

Collect estimates based on decisions made, and update the 2x phases – min 10 days?Time for updates Prec Rs, in both directions – min 7 days?Gap to a hearing – c.7-10 days?
I can see that it wouldn’t be ideal to have the CMH in March, but I can see it happening as a matter of practicality, and it shouldn’t be the end of the world. It would be a fairly
 short and straightforward hearing.
I also doubt that it will really be possible to know exactly how much time will be required until at the Jan 26 CMC and hearing what the judges are deciding needs to be done.
Again, if the impracticalities end up pushing the court away from budgeting (at least in respect of ADR, which is likely to be harder than Experts), is that necessarily a bad thing?
(Also, surely the ADR costs wouldn’t start being incurred until end of April 2026, given they are in Second General?)
 
Whether costs counsel need to attend at the Jan CMC (22-23 Jan 2026)
Unfortunately(?) I am in Mexico from 17-31 Jan, but I will ask the clerks re Ben and Theo.
 
Budgeting framework
Unless it’s something the Ds are keen on, I’d be minded to just keep this as simple as possible. I don’t think this is a variation because there has been no budget set for Experts/ADR
 as phases.
I think the starting point, and probably the simplest answer, is that there would be two fresh phases for Experts and ADR with ‘incurred’ costs running (in the way we have done it
 previously) to the date of CMH3 – save that, for ADR, so long as the hearing was before the end of April, that would actually remain unchanged.
Once set, the ADR phase could be added to an updated Second General quite easily, as the incurred date is likely to be unaffected.
But even for the Experts, I don’t see why that couldn’t be added to the same document as the other T3 phases, once set. It would have a different ‘incurred’ cut off date, but everyone
 would know that (the relevant order would make it clear) and we could add a footnote to the face of the budget for the avoidance of doubt.
Overall, my view is we should (a) keep it simple, and (b) seek to agree our proposed approach with Ds in advance, much like we did on incurred dates previously. I don’t think we should
 decide our approach without knowing what their thoughts on it are.
 
Preparation for Budgeting
Let’s perhaps discuss this on the call.
It seems like there might be some discussions which can be had in advance of the Jan CMC in relation to different foreseeable scenarios to get the ball rolling on information gathering.
 But my first reaction is that these various potential changes, and the likelihood we won’t know which applies until 23 Jan, is why a February 2026 seems a little ambitious to me.
 
Other variations to T2/First General Budgets
I suppose it will depend on what the details of the envisaged variations are, but I am sceptical about whether the court will have any appetite for engaging in questions of variations
 to the T2/G1 budgets at this stage. Surely the costs will all have been incurred by the time any such variation hearing comes to be held (and perhaps even before we make an application)?
If that’s right, the court will surely say that these are questions to be dealt with on the basis of whether there is a ‘good reason to depart’ on assessment, rather than a variation
 (which is intended to be a largely prospective process). See Persimmon Homes Ltd & Anor v Osborne Clark & Anor
[2021] EWHC 831 (Ch), at [134]-[136].
And in any event, we would have to be conscious of the risk that:

The Ds use it as an opportunity to object and definitive close down any hope of recovering the additional costs (rather than leaving open the question of a
 ‘good reason to depart’); andDs might well say their costs have increased too, and seek their own increases to those budgets, with knock-on consequences for ATE levels etc.
 
Looking forward to discussing further at 11:30.

Simon

STRICTLY PRIVATE AND CONFIDENTIAL

Dear all,

I hope you are all well. I write further to my last update on 5 August 2025, to provide you with a brief update on the following matters as they relate to the Ford NOx Emissions Litigation (the “Ford Litigation”), and the Pan-NOx Litigation generally
 (the “Litigation”):


PDD Trial Preparation;
Claimants Mechanical Expert;
Quantum Trial and discontinuance;
Change in personnel.

PDD Trial Preparation and final Pre-Trial Review

We are fast approaching the commencement of the PDD Trial, with the first day of trial listed for 13 October 2025, and the trial due to run until 19 December 2025.

Our skeleton argument was filed and served on 19 September, representing a mammoth undertaking by the entire Solicitor team and the barristers. The Ford specific annex to the skeleton argument was filed and served on 24 September. There was a slight extension
 to the Ford annex on account of the Defendants providing a very late second witness statement from a Ford employee. While we were not obliged to permit this into evidence, we took the view after considering it, that the statement was in fact more helpful for
 us and the case to allow its entry, rather than refusing permissions. As a caveat to our permittance of its inclusion, we agreed a short extension to the Ford annex.

As soon as I am in a position to provide you with a copy of the skeleton argument (with redactions for confidential information) I will send this to you. I would hope this will be later this week. I am extremely pleased with the final version of the skeleton
 argument. Our counsel team have done a remarkable job and it presents the best possible case for the court to consider.

While negotiations on the final timetable continue between the parties, we are close to concluding the timetable.

The first week of trial, due to commence on 13 October 2025, will consist of the Claimants and the Defendants making their opening remarks to the Court, in essence setting the scene, before we then move into evidence on what constitutes Normal Driving Conditions
 and then turning to each individual manufacturer. The order of the manufacturers will be Mercedes, Ford, Peugeot Citroen, Renault and Nissan.

It is expected that the Ford evidence, including the cross examination of experts and witnesses, will start on or around 13 November and run for just over a week.

If any of you are interested in attending Court for any part of the trial, please let us know and we will be able to arrange this with you.

There is due to be a final “Pre-Trial Review” hearing before the Court on 6 October which we are preparing for and this hearing will aim to settle any final issues or disputes that may impact the smooth running of the trial. The parties are in the process of
 agreeing an agenda for this hearing, and we will provide you with a further update on this in due course.

Claimants’ Software and Mechanical Experts

As per my previous update, I confirmed that in a hearing on 10 September, the Court unfortunately did not side with the Claimants in respect of the expert applications, and gave some strict directions with regard to steps the parties were required to take in
 respect of the software evidence that had been prepared.

We have been working hard to prepare and finalise the software report with the redactions / removals as advised by the Court and a version of these amended reports was provided to the Defendants on 24 September. We are awaiting the Defendants’ response to this
 draft report.  

In respect of the Claimants' mechanical expert, the Claimants' barrister team have provided a note to us in which they have flagged certain concerns with the mechanical expert. They have raised that they are concerned how the expert will perform at trial and
 that certain precautions need to be taken with the expert. Importantly, however, they have not told us that these concerns impact on the prospects of success of the case and we remain confident in the case we have prepared against Ford.

We are taking this note incredibly seriously and we are working hard, with the other Lead Solicitors, to prepare the expert for the trial. We are confident that, even with these concerns, the expert will be suitably prepared for trial, having undergone significant
 preparatory work before he takes the stand.

The expert is due to travel to the UK, from America, on 29 September, and will largely be based here, with the team, until his evidence is complete. He will observe various cross-examinations of other experts and will get a good feel for the experience he is
 likely to have in the witness box.

The team will also be assisting him in his preparation.

If you have any questions regarding this, please do let me and the Ford team know.

Quantum Trial

As you are aware, the Court has ordered that a second trial be listed in these NOx Litigations for October 2026. This trial, referred to as the “Quantum Trial” is in relation to the value of certain claims that are being brought by the Claimants. The Court
 will assess what value should be attributed to different heads of loss claimed by the Claimants, each of which were sustained as a result of the Defendants’ conduct, and determine a value for each claim being brought.

The Quantum Trial is proceeding, at least initially, on the basis of assumptions that the vehicles had prohibited defeat devices in them. This is necessary because we will not have a judgment from the Court on the defeat devices until at some point in mid-2026
 (post the October 2025 trial), and it is impractical for the entire litigation to grind to a half while waiting for this judgment. As such, we will prepare evidence and submissions on what we have pleaded for the PDD Trial, and this will then be updated, in
 very short order, once we have that judgment.

It is obviously impractical for the Court to hear evidence and consider losses on an individual basis (to do so would defeat the purpose of a group litigation), and so how this trial will proceed is by way of Sample Claimants. These are Claimants, selected
 between the Claimants and Defendants, who represent a range of characteristics and different issues across the Claimant cohort such that findings by the Court can be applied to all claimants. The characteristics that the Claimants needed to represent were
 included in Annex 2 to the October 2024 CMC Order, a copy of which is attached again for ease.

The process of negotiating these Sample Claimants took some time but the parties have finally reach agreement. A total of 40 Sample Claimants have been negotiated between the Claimants and Defendants across the Pan-NOx Litigations, split as eight per manufacturer,
 and of those eight, four selected by the Claimants, and four by the Defendants. Details of the Ford Sample Claimants can be provided if required.

Over the course of the negotiations, the Defendants made various nominations that the Claimants wished to resist, for various reasons i.e. the Claimants did not wish to participate as Sample Claimants, or they wished to pursue their claim in a different jurisdiction.
 In circumstances where those Sample Claimant nominees did not wish to proceed, the Defendants have taken the position that they must have their claims removed from the English Litigation. We have some sympathy with this, especially where Claimants wish to
 pursue their claim in a different jurisdiction.

Kenneth Gormley is one such person. Mr Gormley is a Ford Claimant, was nominated by the Defendants as a Sample Claimant, however we have since identified he is bringing a claim in both the England & Wales jurisdiction as part of this claim, and also in a separate
 litigation in Scotland.

Mr Gormley cannot continue with both claims and he was required to pick which one he wanted to continue with and we have instructions from Mr Gormley that he wishes to pursue his claim as part of the Scottish proceedings. We therefore are required to prepare
 and serve a formal notice of discontinuance in respect of Mr Gormley’s claim in the English proceedings.

Pursuant to paragraphs 29 and 30 of the Ford Group Litigation Order, we are seeking your instructions to act on Mr Gormley’s instructions and discontinue his claim.

Before confirming these instructions, we must advise you of the effect of this discontinuance. While it will not adversely impact the litigation, indeed the Litigation is already proceeding past this, the discontinuance will necessarily result in the Defendants
 being entitled to incur costs in the Litigation, that will be recoverable by them in due course.

As an initial reassurance, these costs will not be due from you or from any of the Claimants, but they will instead be covered, should they need to be paid, by either the ATE provider who is providing cover for this Litigation, or by Mr Gormley himself.

The general rule, under the governing Civil Procedure Rules 38.6 is that where a Claimant discontinues all or part of their claim, the Defendant has an automatic right to the costs they have incurred in respect of their claim.

There will be two types of costs that the Defendants will be able to recover: common costs, and individual costs.

As explained in the Client Committee meeting post the first Cost Management Hearing, the individual costs will be costs solely in relation to Mr Gormley’s claim, and the common costs will be the apportioned share of the Defendants overall costs of this exercise
 in relation to Mr Gormley’s claim. Mr Gormley’s claim is one claim out of hundreds of thousands, and so while we remain unaware of the level of costs that have been incurred by the Defendants, we believe the overall amount of the common costs will be minimal.

These costs cannot be resolved until the conclusion of the case and so there is no immediate cost that will be required to be paid.

I am of course available to discuss any aspect of this with you before you confirm your instructions, but I wish to reassure you that this discontinuance will not result in you, or any of the other thousands of claimants in the Litigation, being out of pocket.

As a result, we respectfully seek your instructions to:


Proceed to discontinue Mr Gormley’s claim in England & Wales; and
Remove Mr Gormley from the Ford Group Register.

Please confirm by return that you are content for us to take these steps

Change of Personnel

As a final piece of information, it is with regret that I must inform you that I have made the difficult decision to resign from my role at Pogust Goodhead.

I am currently working my notice period, with my final day of employment with the firm still subject to negotiation. As soon as I know when my final day is, I will inform you of this. I appreciate you will need to know this information.

Please rest assured that even with me having made the decision to part from the firm, I will be, and I am, continuing to act in the best interests of the Claimant Committee, and the wider claimant cohort. I personally have devoted a significant amount of time
 to this case and I am determined to ensure that the case is as best presented at trial as it can be.

I must also, at this point, advise you that the Partner with overall conduct of the Pan-NOx Litigations for Pogust Goodhead, Peter Gallagher, has also resigned. I am unable to comment on the reasons for his departure, but he has formally left the firm and the
 firm is putting in place a new head of the NOx department. They will contact you to confirm who this person is in due course. 

The remainder of the Ford Pogust Goodhead team remains in situ and they will continue to liaise with you. I remain with conduct of the matter, and when a decision has been made as to who will take conduct of the matter once I have departed, I will arrange for
 a handover to take place such that you are introduced to the new case lead.

Should you have any questions regarding the contents of this letter, please do not hesitate to contact us.

As always, we are grateful for your continued support and attention to the matter.

Yours faithfully,

Michael & the Ford Litigation Team

Sophia, Jamie and I have prepared three tables:



Schedule 1: Mercedes-only common costs

Schedule 2: All Pan-NOx common costs

Schedule 3: All Lead & ALGLO combined common costs


Total common costs claimed
Each table is divided into the relevant cost budgets, displaying incurred costs (column D) and approved costs (column F) from the First Costs Management Hearing (CMH1) and the Second Costs Management Hearing (CMH2). These figures mirror exactly what

We have also included “Non-Budgeted” cost rows (11, 24, 37), with explanations (column L). These reflect incurred costs of which the Defendants are only partially aware due to interim Statements of Costs etc.

Recovery against common costs claimed
We have applied a 60% recovery rate on all incurred costs (column E). This figure can be adjusted, and the tables will self-calculate.

We have also added adjustments to the approved budgeted costs (column G) to show the pro-rata budgeted amounts we can expect to recover, with explanations (column J).

Liability apportionment on recovered costs
The schedule summary then applies the proposed proportionate share method of apportionment for Mercedes:


100% of Mercedes-only common costs (row 42)

23.68% of Pan-NOx costs (row 43)

44.77% of Lead & ALGLO costs (row 44)


Total common cost settlement
All interim costs awards have then been credited (G46), with details of payment made outlined in the table “Interim Costs Orders Paid.” 

We then divided the adjusted total common cost settlement figure (G67) by the number of claims in the Mercedes Group Register as of 1st October 2025 (428,371) to obtain the total common cost settlement per claim (G68).

Next steps
We expect a call may be the best way to go through the schedule in detail, but in the meantime, two points to consider are:

It is difficult to obtain a complete picture of non-budgeted common costs, and these are, in any event, particularly hard to recover inter partes.

We may need to decide whether to (a) limit non-budgeted costs to the amounts the Defendants are aware of, or (b) include all our non-budgeted totals in the model but use the non-budgeted costs as a concession as part of the negotiations. 

Apportionment:
Which Pan-NOx / Lead & ALGLO apportionment method do we want to adopt? All three options are included in the sheet “Pan NOx, L&A Apportionment” for discussion. We have applied Option 2, the Proportionate Share method, within the table.

Hi PG team, 
 
Further to the con with counsel on 13 November 2025 (note attached), we have drafted a letter to go to the Defendants on the points as advised by counsel.

 
Please can you review and provide any comments/amends. We think it would be sensible to run the draft past Simon T before it goes too.

 
By way of reminder, the key points to be made were:

 
1. Upcoming CMC and Budgeting Exercise
The first point should note the forthcoming CMC in January 2026 (referring to paragraph 126 of the CMH2 judgment) and raise for discussion the scope and form of any further budgeting exercise that may
 be required. It would be helpful to clarify whether there are any applicable deadlines for updating one or both of the T3 Expert Reports or the ADR/Settlement Discussions phase, including how to treat the incurred costs of the T3 Expert Reports.
 
2. Proposed Dates
The second section should explore the floating of potential dates. At this stage, it is recognised that the time required will depend upon the Court’s decision regarding the scope of any further budgeting.
 Nonetheless, it may be constructive to propose an initial exploration of possible dates for a hearing, anticipated to require no more than one day. Dates to avoid will need to be gathered for the entire cost counsel team on both sides, before writing to check
 the Court's availability, including that of Senior Cost Judge Rowley. We propose that the hearing be listed before the end of April, as this would enable the ADR phase to be accommodated prior to the commencement of the Second General Budget.
 
3. ADR Phase and Budgeting Assumptions
The third section should concern the ADR/Settlement Discussions phase. With reference to the relevant paragraphs of the CMH2 judgment, the key issue preventing completion of the budgeting for this phase
 has been the divergence between the parties’ underlying assumptions and expectations. It would therefore be appropriate to invite the Defendants to indicate whether they have any proposals to align or harmonise the assumptions upon which the respective budgets
 are based.
 
Many thanks,
Sophia

Morning Sarah,
 
Ahead of our call to discuss at 11:30am, I just thought I’d flag some initial thoughts on the below, which we can then discuss later.
 
Wording of draft Order
Happy to discuss later this morning, but from my perspective, I’m not too concerned by Ds’ drafting of para 3.
For Experts, it seems to me inevitable that the court will want to budget them once the question of disciplines is resolved (and will want to whatever the wording of the order).
For ADR, wouldn’t it be in the Claimants’ favour
not to budget (given the scale of our estimates, and the likely approach which the court would take to them), if the court had any inclination not to do so? If so, don’t we want to give room for the court to decide that ADR is actually too difficult/uncertain
 to budget at the moment, rather than say they are forced to do so?
If that’s right, I would be inclined to go with Ds’ version of paragraph 3. But happy to discuss on our call.
 
CMH2 Consequentials
This has reminded me – have we had a decision on the CMH costs order yet?
 
Timing of CMH3 (Or CMH2.2, however we want to think of it!)
I agree that if there is to be further budgeting post-January we will need to crack on with it, there’s no point trying to drag our heels.
However, query whether a Feb CMH is a bit ambitious. Presumably we need time, post Jan CMC to:

Collect estimates based on decisions made, and update the 2x phases – min 10 days?Time for updates Prec Rs, in both directions – min 7 days?Gap to a hearing – c.7-10 days?
I can see that it wouldn’t be ideal to have the CMH in March, but I can see it happening as a matter of practicality, and it shouldn’t be the end of the world. It would be a fairly
 short and straightforward hearing.
I also doubt that it will really be possible to know exactly how much time will be required until at the Jan 26 CMC and hearing what the judges are deciding needs to be done.
Again, if the impracticalities end up pushing the court away from budgeting (at least in respect of ADR, which is likely to be harder than Experts), is that necessarily a bad thing?
(Also, surely the ADR costs wouldn’t start being incurred until end of April 2026, given they are in Second General?)
 
Whether costs counsel need to attend at the Jan CMC (22-23 Jan 2026)
Unfortunately(?) I am in Mexico from 17-31 Jan, but I will ask the clerks re Ben and Theo.
 
Budgeting framework
Unless it’s something the Ds are keen on, I’d be minded to just keep this as simple as possible. I don’t think this is a variation because there has been no budget set for Experts/ADR
 as phases.
I think the starting point, and probably the simplest answer, is that there would be two fresh phases for Experts and ADR with ‘incurred’ costs running (in the way we have done it
 previously) to the date of CMH3 – save that, for ADR, so long as the hearing was before the end of April, that would actually remain unchanged.
Once set, the ADR phase could be added to an updated Second General quite easily, as the incurred date is likely to be unaffected.
But even for the Experts, I don’t see why that couldn’t be added to the same document as the other T3 phases, once set. It would have a different ‘incurred’ cut off date, but everyone
 would know that (the relevant order would make it clear) and we could add a footnote to the face of the budget for the avoidance of doubt.
Overall, my view is we should (a) keep it simple, and (b) seek to agree our proposed approach with Ds in advance, much like we did on incurred dates previously. I don’t think we
 should decide our approach without knowing what their thoughts on it are.
 
Preparation for Budgeting
Let’s perhaps discuss this on the call.
It seems like there might be some discussions which can be had in advance of the Jan CMC in relation to different foreseeable scenarios to get the ball rolling on information gathering.
 But my first reaction is that these various potential changes, and the likelihood we won’t know which applies until 23 Jan, is why a February 2026 seems a little ambitious to me.
 
Other variations to T2/First General Budgets
I suppose it will depend on what the details of the envisaged variations are, but I am sceptical about whether the court will have any appetite for engaging in questions of variations
 to the T2/G1 budgets at this stage. Surely the costs will all have been incurred by the time any such variation hearing comes to be held (and perhaps even before we make an application)?
If that’s right, the court will surely say that these are questions to be dealt with on the basis of whether there is a ‘good reason to depart’ on assessment, rather than a variation
 (which is intended to be a largely prospective process). See Persimmon Homes Ltd & Anor v Osborne Clark & Anor
[2021] EWHC 831 (Ch), at [134]-[136].
And in any event, we would have to be conscious of the risk that:

The Ds use it as an opportunity to object and definitive close down any hope of recovering the additional costs (rather than leaving open the question of a ‘good reason to depart’);
 andDs might well say their costs have increased too, and seek their own increases to those budgets, with knock-on consequences for ATE levels etc.
 
Looking forward to discussing further at 11:30.
Thanks,
Simon
