Carmakers Gear Up For Once-In-A-Generation Dieselgate Trial
By Joanne Faulkner 

 
One of the biggest and most complex group claim trials ever seen in the High Court will open Monday as more than a million motorists try to prove that major car manufacturers equipped their vehicles with devices
 designed to cheat emissions rules.


The trial, which is due to last 10 weeks, centers on whether five lead defendants — Mercedes-Benz, Renault, Ford, Nissan and the Peugeot-Citroën
 group — incorporated prohibited "defeat devices" into diesel vehicles.

"This is a once-in-a-generation piece of litigation — both in scale and in its potential impact on corporate accountability," Benjamin Croft, a partner at Leigh Day, the law firm leading the claimants'
 case, said.

The unprecedented litigation has been years in the making, and involves more than 20 law firms, including Pogust Goodhead. Attention on the main trial has been slightly overshadowed by Pogust Goodhead
 taking the unusual step of applying to be removed as co-lead solicitors a week before it was due to start.

Pogust said it did not want recent departures from the firm, including by its co-founder and the head partner on the case, as well as concerns about the role of Gramercy, its litigation-funder, becoming a distraction. But Justice Sara Cockerill, the judge overseeing
 the trial, on Friday dismissed the application, ruling that the implications of approving the plan were "far from clear".

A judging panel is being asked from Monday to look at how emission control systems operated in a sample of 20 vehicles sold between 2012 and 2017. The panel will assess whether those systems had any element of design that amounted to a prohibited defeat device,
 or PDD.

"The case goes to the heart of corporate accountability and environmental justice," Alicia Alinia, CEO at Pogust Goodhead, said. The court will test whether prohibited defeat devices were used to game emissions rules and, if so, what impact they have had on
 the air we all breathe and the health of people exposed to higher levels of harmful pollution."

The claimants say that when PDDs are installed in engine management systems they could detect when the cars were under test conditions and ensure, for those periods, that harmful emissions were kept within legal limits. When the vehicles were driven on the
 road, it is claimed, they produced much higher levels of emissions.

"The trial will determine whether those defeat devices existed, whether they were prohibited, and whether any justifications put forward by the manufacturers stand up," Croft said.

The carmakers are alleged to have misled customers about compliance by some vehicles with nitrogen oxide emissions standards. The companies deny this claim.

The trial is a milestone in the wider emissions claims that have been filed at the High Court against almost every manufacturer of diesel cars. It is referred to as the NOx Emissions Group Litigation or Pan NOx. Together, there are claims by 1.6 million drivers.

The High Court's aim is that a judgment, expected next July, will give guidance to all the manufacturers facing claims, with a view to avoiding the need for any further trials on the presence of prohibited defeat devices in vehicles.

Croft described a defeat device as any element of design which senses temperature, vehicle speed, engine speed and other parameters for the purpose of delaying or deactivating any part of the emission control systems.

There are scenarios in which the use of defeat devices can be justified under European emissions law, Croft said, mainly to protect the engine against damage or accident.

The claimants say that drivers were deceived into buying vehicles marketed as environmentally friendly and compliant with emissions standards. They are seeking damages for breaches of statutory duty and consumer protection laws.

"We're talking about vehicles that, when being driven normally on the roads, emitted up to seven times the legal limit of nitrogen oxides, which are harmful to human health and the environment," Croft said.

The car manufacturers say, on the other hand, that the case put forward on behalf of drivers is flawed and misunderstands the technical realities of diesel engines, and how vehicles' emission control systems are designed and how they operate.

The legal arguments will also examine the real-world conditions in which a car is likely to be driven. This includes factors such as temperature or altitude.

The Pan NOx claims are part of the ongoing fallout from the Dieselgate emissions scandal that rocked Volkswagen AG in 2015. The German carmaker faced litigation in multiple countries after it was
 found to have installed illegal defeat devices to cheat emissions tests.

VW vehicles emitted far higher levels of pollutants during real-world driving than in laboratory tests because of a program in the engine software that sensed when the car was being driven under test conditions.

VW agreed to pay £193 million ($256 million) in 2022 to more than 90,000 drivers in England and Wales to settle High Court claims.

The car manufacturers will argue that their technology not the same as that which was used by the VW group. The engines in the VW case operated differently depending on whether they were undergoing regulatory testing. But Mercedes, for example, says that none
 of its vehicles include any functionality that would sense when they were in test mode and operate in another way.

The carmakers were told in July to release unrestricted documents detailing the operational parameters of alleged defeat devices in the diesel vehicles following a campaign from two environmental campaign
 groups.

Croft said that the ruling will allow the press and the public to see some of the emails and presentations that were being made to senior figures at the manufacturers when the Dieselgate scandal started a decade ago.

Depending on the judgment, a quantum trial to determine compensation is listed for October 2026.

--Editing by Hazel Vidler.
